newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mobutu on ship for Zaire talks, said ready to quit.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu on ship for Zaire talks, said ready to quit.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko joined civil war foe Laurent Kabila on board a customised icebreaker on Sunday and a South African official said the veteran leader had agreed to stand down.

Mobutu, battling cancer and a whirlwind revolt at home, looked grim-faced and sad as he boarded the SAS Outeniqua where Kabila and South Africa's Nelson Mandela had been waiting for him since late Saturday.

With Kabila's forces closing in on the capital Kinshasa, a South African official said Mobutu, one of a vanishing breed of veteran African strongmen, had told negotiators he was prepared to stand down.

"There is an agreement in principle for Mobutu's resignation and the launching of a transitional process," the official, who asked not to be named, told reporters on the South African ship shortly before Mobutu boarded.

Mobutu, who has dominated the sprawling and chaotic nation at the heart of Africa for more than three decades, wore his trade-mark leopard-skin hat. He held his wife Bobi Ladawa's hand. In the other hand, he had his usual carved walking stick.
The New York Times reported in its Sunday edition that Mobutu had written to U.S. President Bill Clinton telling him he was prepared to stand down.
The major issue holding up the resignation appeared to be whether Kabila would take undivided power or share it with other political forces, the newspaper reported.
The Russian-built Outeniqua prepared to leave Congo's port of Pointe Noire once Mobutu was safely on board.
Mobutu aides had envisaged talks focusing on a peaceful transition with elections open to all, rejecting suggestions the meeting is a face-saver to allow him to stand down with dignity.
Kabila, 56, had refused to declare a truce for the talks.

"I have told President Nelson Mandela that Mobutu would have to resign immediately our talks start otherwise my forces are under instructions to move into Kinshasa should he refuse," Kabila told Reuters by satellite telephone from the ship.
Kabila, whose forces took up arms in October and control three quarters of the sprawling nation at the heart of Africa, boarded the ship by helicopter late on Saturday.
One diplomat said the rebel leader had been looking for any excuse not to come. At one point, a frustrated Mandela got on the satellite phone to him and shouted down the line.
Mobutu spent Saturday on shore in Pointe Noire after sailing into international waters with Mandela on Friday for a rendezvous Kabila failed to keep, citing security reasons.

Mobutu, 66, seized power in 1965 and was backed during the Cold War by the United States as a bulwark against Soviet communism. He has seen his hold over the nation of 40 million people broken by Kabila's lightning advances.

Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of fighting alongside Kabila's forces. Independent sources say rebel forces have just captured Mobutu's Lisala birthplace and are marching on Kinshasa and his jungle palace in Gbadolite in the north.

Kabila said he expected his forces to be 80 km (50 miles) from Kinshasa by Sunday evening. Rebel commanders said they were moving up reinforcements and heavy weaponry for a final assault on the city of five million people.
The military governor of the teeming capital asked residents to stay calm in the face of the rebel advance and told security forces to protect its population without discrimination.
The U.S. State Department urged American citizens to leave Zaire and warned them not to travel there citing the "deteriorating security and political situation".
The United States, France, former colonial power Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.

Mobutu boarded the ship with great difficulty on Friday. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a ramp. On Sunday, he and his wife squeezed into a makeshift quayside lift and were hoisted on board.
